rows.description: A talented junior threatens you with faster progress. Notice the sting, then decide: share opportunities, give credit, and keep growing your own skills. Holding them back protects your ego but hurts the team and you.

A younger colleague looks up to you and copies your habits. It is an honour and a responsibility. Be honest about your failures, model integrity, and do not seek adoration or use their trust for your ego.
Seeing your mentee grow makes you proud, and slightly wistful. Celebrate them without claiming credit, and be glad when they surpass you. Good mentors work towards being no longer needed.
A mentee keeps asking you to decide everything. Help them build judgment: ask what they think, offer options, and celebrate independent choices. Rescuing them each time weakens them and burdens you.
I notice that officers treat rich kids gently and poorer boys roughly. I feel anger and helplessness. Wise: record what happened, seek an adult or legal aid, and channel anger into knowing my rights.
I have seen bad police behaviour and I now see every uniform as a threat. Wise: stay careful without hating everyone, and know that many officers do their duty properly.
A friend brags about talking back to police. I feel the pull to copy. Wise: courage is knowing when to stay calm; a video for likes can cost me my safety.
My parent is frightened after I was questioned and turns strict. Wise: listen to the fear, share the full story, and agree on safe habits like sharing locations.
I am scared of the dark and imagine things in the corner. Fear is real even if the danger is not. Talking about it and having a small light helps, and it fades with time.
A friend laughs that I am a scaredy-cat. It stings. Being afraid does not mean I am weak; I can say everyone is afraid of something, and choose friends who do not tease.
My mother sits beside me after a nightmare and says I am safe. Her calm makes my heart slow down. I learn that fear shared becomes smaller.

I see the other side as stupid or evil and enjoy mocking them. Wise: understand their fears, argue the issue and not the person, and keep the moral high ground by being fair. Harmful: dehumanising anyone.
A leader keeps asking for more money and says doubters are traitors. Wise: real movements welcome transparency; ask how funds are used and treat forced unity as a warning sign.

The group is like family, and I hesitate to speak when it makes a bad tactical or ethical choice. Wise: dissent within a movement is loyalty too; say it early and kindly. Harmful: silence that leads to harm.

I give time, energy and hope to a cause I believe in, and it gives my life direction. Wise: keep sleep, studies and relationships intact so the commitment lasts. Harmful: burning out or seeing all non-members as enemies.
I feel I will die without them and need constant reassurance and check-ins. Wise: see this as anxiety and not love, seek support, and build my own interests. Harmful: monitoring or controlling them.
They demand my passwords, tell me what to wear, and get angry when I see friends. It is control and not proof of love. Wise: name it, keep friends close, and tell a trusted adult.
I like them and we both can say no, keep friends, and enjoy the time. Wise: keep communicating openly and treat consent as always on. It grows because neither owns the other.
When I resist, they say I am selfish or that they will fall apart. I feel responsible for their feelings. Wise: care without giving in, and get help from a counsellor or elder if it continues.
I catch someone cheating against me and feel furious. Wise: tell the referee or an adult calmly instead of accusing loudly or retaliating. Cheating back turns me into the same thing.
I could bend the rule and nobody would notice. Winning feels big and losing feels small. A wise child knows a win by cheating feels empty and would need to be hidden. I play fair.
I cheated and won, and the trophy feels heavy. Guilt is my conscience working. I can admit it to the coach, accept a consequence and start clean. Hiding it makes it grow.
